Soviet Intelligence. The secret police and espionage apparatus of the Soviet Union throughout its existence, most famously the KGB, serving as political police, secret service, and intelligence agency. These organizations were instruments of state control, conducting surveillance on the Soviet population, conducting massive counterintelligence operations during the Cold War, and maintaining a vast network of foreign agents worldwide.

The Cheka, established by Vladimir Lenin immediately after the Russian Revolution, was the Soviet Union's first secret police. It evolved through successive reorganizations into the NKVD under Stalin and eventually the KGB under Nikita Khrushchev. Soviet intelligence played a defining role in the Cold War, recruiting deep-cover agents in Western governments, militaries, and intelligence agencies. The Cambridge Five spy ring, which included members of the British upper class, was a spectacular Soviet espionage victory in post-war Britain.

The KGB under Yuri Andropov became a state within the state during the 1970s and 1980s, wielding enormous power over Soviet leadership and conducting pervasive domestic surveillance that created a climate of fear and suspicion among the Soviet population. Soviet intelligence employed extensive networks of informants who reported on neighbors, coworkers, and even family members, making everyday life a landscape of betrayal and suspicion throughout the Soviet era.

The GRU, military intelligence, operated parallel to the KGB, conducting espionage missions globally and recruiting military attachés and defectors. The two agencies competed for resources and sometimes clashed in their operations. Soviet defectors including Oleg Penkovskiy, Andrei Sakharov, and Vitaly Shcherbakov risked their lives to expose Soviet espionage operations and internal repression to the West, fundamentally shaping Western understanding of Soviet threats.
